judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: The panicked opening is lively and Nox-like, but it points the way through a chain of landmarks ('west of the [Thing] behind the old sundial'), and the backstory about who drove the creatures off the hill is more causal tidiness than Westwood usually bothers with.

items.label: B
items.critique: The voice is warm and the 'make heads or tails of it' aside is pleasant, but it repeats the 'west of X past Y' direction formula, adds world detail ('Nobody can set a net out there now', 'my boys and me could fish again'), and closes on a neat reward-as-promised.

items.label: C
items.critique: The mock-grand diction ('beset', 'abominable creatures', 'liberated') and the dud-bow joke could be Westwood's, but the bow anecdote is the same template as H, which suggests one writer working a formula.

items.label: D
items.critique: The absurd premise (a frog trapped in a burning house) and the player's cheeky reply implied through 'Loads and loads of money?' are pure Nox humour, with short exclamatory lines and '?!'.

items.label: E
items.critique: It starts mid-conversation ('Actually, business has been somewhat slow'), says 'lad' and 'young sir', and pays '100 in gold' with an ellipsis. That is Westwood's innkeeper register, a little wordy but authentic.

items.label: F
items.critique: The fussy cartographer is a neat comic sketch, but the 'I take it you have read my notice?' set-up, the tidy list of complaints and '100 gold pieces, and well earned' read as a polished modern pastiche rather than Westwood's blunter lines.

items.label: G
items.critique: The repeated 'mate', 'damn fine spell', the boots stolen while bathing, and a long, literal journal entry ('...and return them to him') all fit Westwood's slightly clumsy, cheerful plainness.

items.label: H
items.critique: The bureaucratic comedy ('authorised', 'expungement of the bears') is over-written, the British spelling stands out, the directions are stacked ('south of the crossroads past the old well'), and the dragon-bow anecdote is padded with an extra punchline.

items.label: I
items.critique: 'Young sir', the double dashes, 'dead or alive', the long gushing thanks and '500 in gold!' are Westwood's Ix-style bounty voice, including its awkward 'single handedly'.

items.label: J
items.critique: It is a story-carrying quest with a mentor's 'Hmmm... Yes.', a robe found instead of a rescue, and a teleporter handoff. The odd self-introduction mid-speech is a typical Westwood seam.

tells: New texts give directions as a chain of landmarks ('west of the village past the drying racks', 'south of the crossroads past the old well'); Westwood says 'east of here' or simply names the place.
New texts set up the quest with tidy cause and effect (who drove the monsters, why the road or the fishing matters); Westwood states the problem and moves on.
New texts reuse one joke template: a reward item with a dubious provenance anecdote, then a dry undercut. Westwood's humour is more random and situational (the frog, 'Loads and loads of money?').

Westwood pays rewards in a fixed formula ('100 in gold!', '500 in gold!') and uses 'young sir', 'lad', double dashes, ellipses and '?!'. The new texts say '100 gold pieces, and well earned' or 'as I promised' in cleaner prose.
Over-elevated or bureaucratic vocabulary ('expungement', 'authorised', 'liberated') and British spelling are a giveaway; Westwood's elevated words are fewer and its American spelling is consistent.
